settings.title: I help creative people make steady work without burning out.

settings.editor:
Ten years ago I was a magazine editor who answered email at midnight and hadn’t written a word of her own in years. I rebuilt my working life around slow mornings, small daily practice and honest limits — and finished two books along the way.

Now I teach the same approach to anyone who suspects there is a kinder way to do ambitious work.

settings.title: Hello, I’m Jade. I believe good work can feel good, too.

settings.editor: Writer, teacher and coach. Former magazine editor. Gardener with mixed results. I live by the sea with my partner, two children and a very loud cat.

For a decade I edited other people’s words for a living and told myself my own writing could wait. It waited eleven years. When burnout finally made the decision for me, I left the magazine with a notebook, a small savings account and no plan at all.

What I found, slowly, was a way of working built on three things: a short creative practice every morning, honest limits on everything else, and a community of people doing the same. It worked for me, then for friends, then for the first fifty students of a course I nearly didn’t launch.
Eleven years of deadlines ended with a long walk and a new notebook.
“Small Mornings” came out and quietly found its readers.
Fifty students in the first cohort; more than 4,000 since.
Working on book three, and with eight coaching clients at a time.

posts.title: The twenty-minute morning
posts.excerpt: Why the smallest daily habit I know has done more for my work than any productivity system.
posts.content:
Every morning, before I open my email, I sit down for twenty minutes with whatever I am making. Not an hour. Not “until I feel inspired”. Twenty minutes, with a kitchen timer, a cup of coffee and the phone in another room.

It sounds too small to matter. That is exactly why it works. Twenty minutes is short enough that I never have a good excuse to skip it, and long enough to write a page, sketch a idea or untangle one stubborn paragraph.

Small, every day, beats big, sometimes

Over a year those mornings add up to more than 120 hours of focused work — more than most of us manage in our occasional heroic weekends. And because the habit is gentle, it survives bad weeks, sick children and deadlines.

You do not need more time. You need a small, protected time that is yours.

Try it for two weeks. Same time, same place, same twenty minutes. Then write and tell me what you made.

posts.title: How to rest without feeling guilty
posts.excerpt: Rest isn’t a reward for finishing. It’s part of the work — here is how I learned to believe that.
posts.content:
For years I treated rest like dessert: something I could have once the real work was done. The real work was never done, so I never rested — and my ideas grew thinner every month.

Three kinds of rest

  • Stillness — a walk with no podcast, ten minutes on a bench, a bath.
  • Play — something absorbing with no goal: a puzzle, a garden, a game with the kids.
  • Company — time with people who know you outside your work.

I now schedule all three into my week as firmly as client calls. My output didn’t drop. It got better, and it got kinder.

posts.title: What I learned launching my first course
posts.excerpt: Fifty students, three mistakes and the one thing I’d do exactly the same way again.
posts.content:
I nearly didn’t launch The Slow Studio. The videos weren’t polished, the workbook had typos and I was certain nobody would pay for it. Fifty people did — and taught me more than I taught them.

Three mistakes

  1. Making the lessons too long. Fifteen minutes is plenty.
  2. Launching without a community space; students wanted each other.
  3. Pricing for the person I was afraid of, not the person I was serving.

One thing I’d repeat

I asked every student, personally, what they hoped to make. Then I built the next lesson around their answers. Nothing I have done since has worked better.

posts.title: A reading list for slow, ambitious people
posts.excerpt: Nine books that changed how I think about time, attention and making things that last.
posts.content:
People ask me for book recommendations more than anything else. These are the nine I give away most often — books about time, attention and the long, quiet patience of good work.

  • A memoir by a potter who threw one bowl a day for thirty years
  • An essay collection on walking as a way of thinking
  • A gardener’s diary that is secretly about patience
  • A short guide to deep reading in a distracted age
  • A novel about a lighthouse keeper and the letters he never sent

Read slowly. Underline freely. And if one of them speaks to you, pass it on to someone who needs it.

posts.title: Saying no, kindly
posts.excerpt: The three-sentence email that protects my mornings — and keeps my relationships warm.
posts.content:
Every yes to someone else’s project is a no to your own. That’s not selfish; it is simple arithmetic. The trick is saying no in a way that leaves the door open and the relationship intact.

My three-sentence no

  1. Thank them, sincerely and specifically.
  2. Say no clearly, without a long excuse.
  3. Offer one small, real alternative if you have one.

“Thank you for thinking of me for this — I love what you’re building. I can’t take it on this season. Could I share it with my newsletter instead?”

Keep a copy in your drafts. You will use it more than you think, and you will feel lighter every time.
